scope: Modern unit timelines 1946–present for the Natural Earth admin-0 units of the audit regions northern-america and central-america: BLZ, CLP, CRI, GTM, HND, MEX, NIC, PAN, SLV (central-america) and BMU, CAN, GRL, SPM, USA (northern-america). Every unit was checked for decolonisation, renames, transfers, occupations and claims since 1945, and NE footprints were compared with the history (island ownership, the NIC/CRI line, Hans Island, Swan Islands, Sapodilla Cayes, uncovered minor islands). Tier-1 overlays: Guatemalan claim to Belize, Sapodilla Cayes, Swan Islands, Gulf of Fonseca islands (El Tigre, Meanguera; 1980–1991), Hans Island; indigenous comarcas of Panama. Note entries record editorial decisions, sub-granularity events and known gaps (Nicaraguan administration north of the Coco to 1961, El Salvador–Honduras bolsones, islands NE leaves outside admin-0, US reservations, Canadian, Central American and Mexican indigenous lands). Audited 2026-10-01 by agent:audit-modern-north-central-america; analysis scripts in .cache/audit/audit-modern-north-central-america.

units.label: Clipperton Island

state.name: Clipperton Island
state.note: French possession by the arbitral award of King Victor Emmanuel III (1931), accepted by Mexico (constitution amended 18 January 1934). Administered by the High Commissioner in French Polynesia until 21 February 2007, then directly by the Minister of Overseas France. Uninhabited since the last US Navy weather-station staff left on 21 October 1945.

units.notes: Natural Earth's HND footprint is the post-1961 / post-1992 territory. (1) Great Swan Island (1.7 km2, inside NE's HND polygon) was held by the United States until the 1971 treaty came into force in 1972 (subunit; disputed overlay m-north-central-america-swan-islands). Little Swan Island (0.49 km2) is not in NE's HND polygon; the coast step gives it to the holder of Great Swan, 2.8 km away. (2) About 8,700 km2 north of the Coco River (today's Gracias a Dios) stayed under Nicaraguan administration until 1961; its line is not described by any source found, so it is not drawn (m-north-central-america-0002). (3) The 'bolsones' disputed with El Salvador until the ICJ judgment of 11 September 1992 are not drawn (m-north-central-america-0003). El Tigre (Honduras) and Meanguera/Meanguerita (El Salvador) are already on the right sides in NE; their 1980–1991 dispute is drawn as overlays m-north-central-america-el-tigre and m-north-central-america-meanguera. (4) The cays north of 15°N found Honduran by the ICJ in 2007 and the Vivorillo cays are outside NE's polygons (m-north-central-america-0014).

units.label: Panama

state.name: Panama Canal Zone
state.note: Administered by the United States under the 1903 Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty, which gave it rights "as if it were sovereign" (Panama kept titular sovereignty); reported to the UN as a non-self-governing territory in 1946–1947. Abolished on 1 October 1979 under the Torrijos–Carter Treaties; the canal itself passed to Panama on 31 December 1999. Approximate boundary: 5 miles each side of the canal centreline and 3 miles out to sea, Gatun Lake to the 100-ft contour and Madden Lake included, the cities of Panama and Colón excluded.

The islands' legal situation was in dispute from the 1980 Lima peace treaty until 1992: overlays m-north-central-america-meanguera (Salvadoran-held, claimed by Honduras) and m-north-central-america-el-tigre (Honduran-held, claimed by El Salvador); Conejo Island, still disputed, is not in NE land (m-north-central-america-0022). The Salvadoran occupation of Honduran territory in the Football War (14 July – 2 August 1969) ended within the year.

state.name: Bermuda
state.note: British colony; officially a 'British Dependent Territory' from 1 January 1983 and a 'British Overseas Territory' since the 2002 Act. On the UN list of non-self-governing territories since 1946. Independence was rejected in the referendum of 16 August 1995 (74% no). The US military presence (from the Second World War) lasted until 1995 and was no transfer of sovereignty.

Labrador's boundary is the 1927 Privy Council line, never formally recognised by Quebec; control unchanged. Internal changes are not drawn: Nunavut was separated from the Northwest Territories on 1 April 1999 (m-north-central-america-0016). Hans Island lies in NE's GRL unit. entries.reason: Editorial decisions for this file. (a) pids: ne:<code> for every unit that exists today, including dependencies (ne:bmu, ne:grl, ne:spm, ne:clp, with kind 'dependency' and power = the administering state); ovr: pids for former dependencies (ovr:british-honduras – one pid across the 1973 rename to Belize –, ovr:dominion-of-newfoundland, ovr:territory-of-alaska, ovr:territory-of-hawaii, ovr:panama-canal-zone). (b) The territories of Alaska and Hawaii (1946–1958) and the Panama Canal Zone are 'dependency' because the United States reported them to the UN as non-self-governing territories (GA res. 66 (I), 1946). (c) Greenland stays 'dependency' of Denmark for 1953–1978 although the 1953 constitution made it an integral county (amt) of Denmark: kept as one Danish-coloured unit so the 1953, 1979 and 2009 status changes show as periods; the period notes say what each status was. Likewise Saint Pierre and Miquelon stays a French 'dependency' (ne:spm) in its years as an overseas department (1976–1984), with periods at its 1976, 1985 and 2003 status changes. (d) Great Swan Island (1946–1971) is given to the United States itself (ne:usa) in tier 0 with a tier-1 'disputed' overlay, because it had no separate government. (e) Tier-1 'disputed' overlays: controller = the tier-0 holder, claimants = the states contesting it.

entries.reason: KNOWN GAP – Nicaraguan administration north of the Coco River until 1961. The 1906 award of the King of Spain made the Coco (Segovia, Wanks) the boundary, but Nicaragua rejected it and kept administering land north of the river. Honduras created the department of Gracias a Dios there in February 1957, which led to the Mocorón clashes (May 1957). The ICJ upheld the award on 18 November 1960. Under the OAS Basis of Arrangement of March 1961, Nicaraguan authorities evacuated about 8,700 km2 (IBS 36; 'more than eight thousand square kilometres' in Nicaragua's 2001 memorial), which Honduras took over by May 1961; a further 17.5 km2 at Teotecacinte was settled on 5 August 1961. Natural Earth's HND unit therefore shows Honduras in 1946–1960 on land Nicaragua held. Not drawn because no source found describes the line of Nicaraguan administration. The 1931 Irías–Ulloa protocol (approved by Nicaragua, never in force) described Nicaragua's claim as the whole left-bank basin of the Coco plus a straight line from the headwaters of the Awawas to the mouth of the Cruta; that is a claim, not proof of administration. To fix it, find a map of the 1957–1961 situation (the OAS Inter-American Peace Committee report of 16 July 1963, OEA/Ser.L/III/II.9, has the Basis of Arrangement and the Mixed Commission minutes), then add an HND subunit for 1946–1960 held by ne:nic.

entries.reason: Panama Canal Zone polygon (PAN subunit, 1946–1978): approximate construction from the treaty definition, checked against two georeferenced US government maps. (1) Canal centreline = Natural Earth 'Panama Canal' centrelines (ne_10m_rivers_lake_centerlines), extended along the dredged approach channels to the Limón Bay breakwater (79.920 W) and the Pacific channel past Flamenco Island (to 8.898 N 79.540 W), then 3 marine miles out to sea. (2) A band 5 statute miles (8,046.72 m) each side with square ends. (3) Plus Natural Earth's Gatun Lake widened by 300 m for the 100-ft contour ('Canal Zone boundary line follows 100 ft. contour around Gatun Lake' – 1920 map). (4) Plus Madden Lake (Alhajuela, 1935), digitized from the 1947 Army Map Service sheet (59 km2) and widened by 150 m for the ~260-ft contour named on that sheet, and the Chagres River corridor from the band to Madden Dam (300 m buffer). (5) Minus the city of Colón (north part of Manzanillo Island) and the city of Panama east of the Curundú line (79°32.2'W 9°02.2'N to 79°33.8'W 8°57.2'N, read off the 1920 map). Result: 1,370 km2 on NE land (official total 1,432 km2 including water). Compared with the 1920 map the band edges lie within about 1 km of the drawn boundary (west edge on 80°00'W, east edge near 79°51'W at the Atlantic; Arraiján just outside). Not drawn: the Colón corridor (1950) and the small 1955 Remón–Eisenhower land returns. After 1 October 1979 the zone ceased to exist and Panama took jurisdiction; until 31 December 1999 the United States kept canal operating areas and defence sites under the treaties. These were scattered parcels without an open map, so they are not drawn and the land shows as Panama from 1979. Sources are public-domain US government maps (1920 Panama Canal map signed by Governor Chester Harding; 1947 US Army Map Service), georeferenced on their printed graticules; scripts in .cache/audit/audit-modern-north-central-america (a05–a08).

entries.reason: KNOWN GAP – American Indian reservations (tribal nations' lands) are not drawn in the modern layer. Public-domain geometry exists (US Census TIGER/Line AIANNH, also served by TIGERweb), but current boundaries cannot simply be back-dated to 1946. Each reservation needs a legal history first: Navajo–Hopi (the 1882 Executive Order Hopi reservation of 16 December 1882, the Joint Use Area, the 1974 and 1996 partition acts); diminishment and disestablishment rulings (e.g. Rosebud, Lake Traverse, Yankton, Uintah and Ouray, Osage); terminations (Menominee 1961–1973; Klamath, terminated 1954 and restored as a tribe in 1986 without land, so its reservation of 1946–1960 is missing from current data); and McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020), after which the Muscogee and other eastern Oklahoma reservations are recognised as never disestablished. The 46 federal reservations of 1,000 km2 or more in the Census 2020 layer (GEOID, land km2): Navajo Nation 2430R 58,370; Uintah and Ouray 4390R 17,540; Tohono O'odham Nation 4200R 11,535; Pine Ridge 2810R 11,248; Cheyenne River 0605R 11,031; Standing Rock 3970R 9,242; Crow 0845R 9,233; Wind River 4610R 8,978; Fort Peck 1250R 8,517; San Carlos 3355R 7,517; Fort Apache 1140R 6,799; Hopi 1505R 6,558; Blackfeet 0305R 6,143; Osage 2595R 5,819; Yakama Nation 4690R 5,576; Colville 0760R 5,480; Flathead 1110R 5,014; Hualapai 1545R 4,121; Lake Traverse 1860R 3,753; Rosebud 3235R 3,596; Fort Berthold 1160R 3,417; Jicarilla Apache Nation 1700R 3,409; Nez Perce 2445R 3,094; White Earth 4595R 2,833; Southern Ute 3925R 2,744; Warm Springs 4545R 2,617; Leech Lake 1940R 2,521; Fort Belknap 1150R 2,511; Ute Mountain 4470R 2,303; Red Lake 3100R 2,288; Fort Hall 1185R 2,108; Laguna Pueblo 1840R 1,987; Mescalero 2205R 1,863; Northern Cheyenne 2490R 1,805; Yankton 4700R 1,723; Zuni 4785R 1,706; Gila River 1310R 1,511; Pyramid Lake Paiute 3010R 1,439; Walker River 4515R 1,368; Coeur d'Alene 0705R 1,357; Colorado River 0735R 1,185; Duck Valley 0965R 1,166; Oneida Nation (NY) 2555R 1,096; Crow Creek 0855R 1,094; Acoma Pueblo 0010R 1,070; Spirit Lake 3935R 1,009. Recommended: a dedicated modern indigenous-overlay pass, coordinated with the 1945 extents the historical northern-america file uses, with one tier-1 'indigenous' overlay per reservation (approximate, period breaks at the legal changes above). Not polities and not to be drawn as such: the Alaska Native regional corporations of 1971 (Metlakatla's Annette Islands Reserve, ~350 km2, is Alaska's only reservation) and the Hawaiian Home Lands.

entries.reason: KNOWN GAP – Nicaragua's Caribbean coast. (a) The Autonomy Statute (Law 28, approved September 1987) created the North and South Atlantic (Caribbean Coast) Autonomous Regions for the coast's peoples (Miskitu, Mayangna, Rama, Garifuna, Creole, mestizo). They are NE admin-1 units NI-AN and NI-AS, but they are multi-ethnic regional governments, not indigenous polities, so they are not drawn as indigenous overlays. (b) Under Law 445 (2003) the Miskitu, Mayangna, Rama and Afro-descendant communities received titles to 23 territories, about a third of the country. That is the real indigenous land map, but no open geometry was found; not drawn.

Costa Rica: 24 indigenous territories under the Indigenous Law of 1977 (Bribri, Cabécar, Ngäbe, Boruca, Térraba, Maleku, Huetar, Chorotega), 3,344 km2 (5.9%) in total. Panama, beyond the three NE-admin-1 comarcas drawn here: Madungandí (Law 24 of 12 January 1996, ~2,076 km2, above granularity), Wargandí (Law 34 of 25 July 2000, 956 km2), Naso Tjër Di (Law 188 of 4 December 2020, 1,606 km2). Belize: Maya customary land tenure in the Toledo District, upheld by the Caribbean Court of Justice (consent order of 22 April 2015; judgment of 30 October 2015), not yet demarcated. Mexico: the Zapatista autonomous municipalities and caracoles in Chiapas (since the 1994 uprising, reorganised in 2023) are de facto self-governing communities without fixed boundaries; ejidos and agrarian communities are tenure, not polities.

entries.reason: Conejo Island (Isla Conejo, Gulf of Fonseca, 13°20′52″N 87°44′34″W): a small islet administered by Honduras (department of Valle) with a military post and claimed by El Salvador (La Unión). El Salvador had asked the ICJ Chamber to settle every island of the Gulf, but the 1992 judgment ruled only on El Tigre, Meanguera and Meanguerita, and the dispute over Conejo continues. Not drawn because the islet is not in Natural Earth's land (nearest NE land, the Honduran coast, is 1.7 km away). If a future land layer includes it, leave it to Honduras with a 'disputed' overlay (claimant ne:slv).
